summary: A canyon cut half a mile deep into red and cream Navajo Sandstone by the Virgin River in southwestern Utah. Hike up the river itself in the Narrows, climb the chained ridge of Angels Landing, or drive the switchbacks and tunnel of the east side. Utah's first national park.
story: Zion is a cross-section. Nine formations of sedimentary rock stand stacked in its walls, and the thickest of them, the Navajo Sandstone, was once a sand sea the size of a small country — dunes that hardened, grain on cemented grain, to more than two thousand feet of pale rock. The Virgin River has spent the last few million years cutting down through all of it as the Colorado Plateau rose beneath, which is why the canyon is so much deeper than the river is wide.

That depth is also the park's ecology. From the canyon floor at around 3,700 feet to the high plateau at 8,700, Zion crosses from desert through pinyon and juniper to stands of fir and aspen, so a day's walk can pass through communities that would otherwise be hundreds of miles apart. Where water seeps out along the contact between porous sandstone and the shale beneath it, hanging gardens grow straight off vertical rock — ferns, columbine and monkeyflower on a cliff face, fed by rain that fell centuries ago.

People have lived in and around the canyon for thousands of years, farming its floor and quarrying its rim. The Southern Paiute knew the upper canyon as Mukuntuweap. Mormon settlers moved in during the 1860s, and it was one of them, Isaac Behunin, who gave the canyon the name that stuck. Federal protection followed in 1909, as a national monument; Congress made it a national park ten years later.

What has changed since is mostly the number of people. The Zion–Mount Carmel Highway brought cars over the east rim in 1930; by the end of the century the canyon road could not hold them, and since 2000 a shuttle has carried visitors up it instead. Angels Landing, the park's most famous and most exposed route, now runs on a permit lottery.

sights.name: Angels Landing
sights.note: A fin of Navajo sandstone reached by switchbacks and a chained ridge, 1,500 feet above the canyon floor.

sights.name: The Narrows
sights.note: The Virgin River's slot canyon, in places twenty feet wide between thousand-foot walls. Walked in the river itself.

sights.name: Observation Point
sights.note: The canyon's highest viewpoint, looking down on Angels Landing.

sights.name: Emerald Pools
sights.note: Three stepped pools fed by seeps and a hanging garden of ferns.

sights.name: Court of the Patriarchs
sights.note: Three sandstone peaks named for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

sights.name: Weeping Rock
sights.note: An alcove where water that fell as rain centuries ago seeps from the rock face.

sights.name: Canyon Overlook
sights.note: A short walk off the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway to a ledge above Pine Creek.

sights.name: Kolob Canyons
sights.note: The park's quiet north-west corner: red finger canyons cut into the Kolob Terrace.

entrances: South Entrance at Springdale — the main way in, and the shuttle's starting point
East Entrance on the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway, through the 1930 tunnel
Kolob Canyons Entrance off Interstate 15 at exit 40, forty miles north
planYourVisit.reservations: The Zion Canyon Scenic Drive is served by a mandatory shuttle for most of the year, and private vehicles are not allowed on it while the shuttle runs. Angels Landing requires a permit from a seasonal lottery, drawn months ahead with a smaller day-before draw.
permits: Angels Landing — permit lottery, one of the few named hikes in the system that needs one
The Narrows top-down, and every wilderness overnight — wilderness permit
Canyoneering routes including the Subway — permit
camping: Watchman Campground, open all year, reservable
Lava Point Campground, primitive, six sites, seasonal
lodging: Springdale, immediately outside the south entrance
seasonalClosures: Kolob Terrace Road and the road to Lava Point close with snow
The Narrows closes when the Virgin River runs high, most often during spring snowmelt

chronology.text: Farmers of the Virgin branch of the Ancestral Puebloan culture work the canyon floor.
Nephi Johnson, scouting for Mormon settlement, enters Zion Canyon.
Isaac Behunin homesteads in the canyon and gives it the name Zion.
President Taft proclaims Mukuntuweap National Monument.
The monument is enlarged and renamed Zion.
The Zion–Mount Carmel Highway opens, with a mile-long tunnel through the cliff.
A shuttle replaces private cars on the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive.
Angels Landing moves to a permit lottery.

safety: Flash floods kill in Zion's slot canyons, and the storm that causes one can be miles away and out of sight. Check the day's flash-flood potential at a visitor centre before entering The Narrows or any canyoneering route, and turn back if the water darkens or rises.
Angels Landing is an exposed scramble along a chained ridge with long drops on both sides. It is not a route to attempt in wind, ice or a hurry.
Canyon temperatures regularly pass 38°C in summer. Carry more water than feels necessary, and walk the long routes early.
regulations: Drones may not be launched, landed or flown in the park.
Dogs are allowed only on the Pa'rus Trail and in developed areas, on a leash.
Stay on trail and on rock: the cryptobiotic crust that holds the desert soil together takes decades to rebuild once broken.
